## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="m5-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Sizing as a mixed-integer program</dt><dd>Solar and battery sizes are continuous; generator sets come whole. One model holds a normal year of 12 average days and the storm's 72 hours.</dd>
<dt>Branch and bound</dt><dd>The relaxation may buy part of a set; splitting into fewer and more sets, and pruning, proves the best whole number.</dd>
<dt>No prices</dt><dd>HiGHS returns no duals for a mixed-integer program; what carrying the hospital costs is the difference between two solved plans.</dd>
<dt>Check and test</dt><dd>The plan is run again with whole sets and their 30% minimum, then on ten drawn winter outages.</dd>
<dt>Rolling horizon</dt><dd>Re-planning every 6 hours on a forecast shows what a plan sized with perfect foresight loses when the sun surprises it.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The sizing model in symbols</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Sizes $S$ (kW of solar), $B$ (kWh of battery, power $B/4$) and $N \in \{0, 1, \dots, 4\}$ (generator sets of 200 kW). For each average day $m$ (weight $w_m$, its month's days) and hour $h$: import $i$, export $e$, solar used $s$, charge $c$, discharge $d$, stored $q$. For each storm hour $t$: $s_t, c_t, d_t, q_t$, generator output $g_t$ and optional loads served $o_t$.

$$\min\; a_S S + a_B B + a_N N + a_F F + \sum_m w_m \sum_h \big(r_h\, i_{m,h} - x\, e_{m,h}\big)$$

$$s + d + i = c + e + 1{,}200, \quad s \le \sigma_{m,h} S, \quad q_{m,h} = q_{m,h-1} + 0.9\,c - d, \quad c, d \le B/4,\; q \le B,\; i \le \bar I,\; e \le \bar E$$

$$s_t + d_t + g_t = c_t + o_t + L^{\text{must}}, \quad q_{-1} = B, \quad g_t \le 200\,N, \quad \textstyle\sum_t 0.07\, g_t \le F$$

$a_S, a_B, a_N$ are each item's cost a year (capital $\times$ the capital recovery factor at the owner's real rate, plus upkeep), $a_F F$ the tank for $F$ gallons, $r_h$ the tariff in hour $h$ (\$/kWh), $x$ the export credit, $\sigma$ the sun per kW, $L^{\text{must}}$ the must-stay-on load (400 kW here). The check adds $g_t \ge 60\,u_t$ and $g_t \le 200\,u_t$ with $u_t \in \{0, \dots, N\}$ sets on, and lets every load be partly served, with unserved must-stay-on load weighted first.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Why the gap and the tie rule matter here</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The sizing asks HiGHS to stop only within 0.0001% of the best bound, so two plans that differ by a few dollars a year are not passed off as one ([HiGHS options](https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/dev/options/definitions/), `mip_rel_gap`). The check's hourly schedule is not unique: the battery can often cover an hour now or later at the same total. Its objective therefore adds small, stated weights (earlier hours first, the list order within a priority, then fuel and battery use), and the page reports only totals that those weights fix. A run stopped by its time limit shows its gap and says it is not proven.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this model leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Prices of any kind from the model: a mixed-integer program has no duals.</li>
<li>The campus's wiring and protection, voltage and frequency inside the island (lesson <a href="f07-microgrids.html">F7</a> shows who forms the island).</li>
<li>Part-load fuel use (a lightly loaded set burns more per kWh), start-up limits and a set that fails to start.</li>
<li>Battery wear, fuel deliveries during the storm, and how often outages happen.</li>
<li>Loads that change through the day: every load is flat here.</li>
</ul>
<p>Modeler's note: <a href="m07-monte-carlo.html">M7</a> samples uncertain inputs with Monte Carlo, and M8 (upcoming) decides before the uncertainty resolves.</p>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m5-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="prices" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The sizing MILP tells you the price of one more kWh of battery.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A mixed-integer program returns no duals. To value a change, size the plan twice, with and without it, and subtract.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="foresight" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A plan that carries the hospital through the storm in the sizing model will carry it in real operation too.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The sizing knows the coming sun. In step 7, a controller that plans on yesterday's sun runs the battery down too early and leaves must-stay-on loads short.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="relax" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If the relaxation buys 1.3 generator sets, no plan with whole sets can cost less than the relaxation.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Whole sets only add a rule to the relaxation, so its cost is a lower bound for every whole-set plan.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m5">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="value" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">How does this lesson put a number on what carrying the hospital through the storm costs?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">From the dual of the storm's energy balance</li><li data-value="b">From the price of diesel</li><li data-value="c">By sizing the plan with and without the storm, and subtracting</li><li data-value="d">It cannot be put in numbers</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>By sizing twice and subtracting: the difference between two solved plans, which is not a price.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="test" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">The plan rides through all ten drawn winter outages. What can you claim?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">It will survive any winter outage</li><li data-value="b">It passed these ten tests, with the model's assumptions</li><li data-value="c">It fails one outage in ten years</li><li data-value="d">It is the cheapest plan for every outage</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Only that it passed these ten tests. Ten drawn outages are a teaching sample, not outage statistics.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:supply-chain-mg"><p>When each facility can install its own wind, solar and storage and trade energy with the grid, a candidate site's renewable resource affects its operating cost.</p><p>Transactive energy, time-of-use tariffs and climate conditions played a critical role in locating factories, warehouses, wind turbines, solar photovoltaics and energy storage systems.</p><p>Contrary to intuition, energy storage systems, which balance intermittent power and uncertain load, had limited benefits for cost saving.</p><p>A mixed-integer model opens factories and warehouses, routes products and sizes each open site's wind, solar and storage, with an hourly energy balance and grid trade. Uncertain weekly store demand enters as a chance constraint with a set service level, written as its deterministic equivalent, so the model stays a mixed-integer linear program.</p><p>Holds when: stylized networks with synthetic distances and costs, candidate sites in California, Arizona and Nevada, and one year, planned week by week for products and hour by hour for energy. Leaves out: grid outages, which the studies do not model.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2023), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apm.2023.02.014">Applied Mathematical Modelling</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<ul class="m5-links">
<li>Open code: <a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/supply-chain-microgrid-models">supply-chain-microgrid-models</a> on GitHub.</li>
<li>Builds on: <a href="m02-unit-commitment.html">M2</a> (whole numbers and branch and bound), <a href="sb1-microgrid-workbench.html">the Microgrid Workbench</a> (the same engine), <a href="f07-microgrids.html">F7</a> and <a href="a14-microgrid-value.html">A14</a> (the campus and its value) and <a href="09-storage.html">lesson 9</a> (storage).</li>
<li>Applied in: the capstone <a href="c1-keep-the-campus-running.html">C1</a>. Open tools for larger models: <a href="https://docs.pypsa.org/">PyPSA</a>, <a href="https://www.pyomo.org/">Pyomo</a> and <a href="https://jump.dev/">JuMP</a>.</li>
</ul>
